case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a multiemployer pension plan may retroactively change the actuarial interest-rate (and related) assumptions used to calculate an employer’s ERISA/MPPAA withdrawal liability after the valuation year, thereby increasing the assessed withdrawal liability for a past withdrawal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA as amended by the Multiemployer Pension Plan Amendments Act of 1980 (MPPAA), principally 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1405 (withdrawal liability), including the statutory requirement that withdrawal liability be determined under the plan’s actuarial assumptions and methods used for funding purposes and be actuarially reasonable (commonly litigated under 29 U.S.C. § 1393).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (M&K Employee Solutions and related entities) argue that the Fund unlawfully recalculated M&K’s withdrawal liability by retroactively revising the interest-rate assumption (and/or associated actuarial inputs) after the relevant plan year to increase the amount owed. In their view, MPPAA ties withdrawal-liability calculations to the plan’s assumptions and methods in effect for the valuation year used for funding, and it does not permit later ‘do-overs’ that change the economic assumptions for a past withdrawal. They emphasize predictability and reliance interests—employers should be able to know the rules and rates that will govern liability at the time of withdrawal—and contend that allowing retroactive assumption changes invites opportunistic manipulation and undermines the statutory design. Petitioners rely heavily on Second Circuit authority (notably Metz) and arbitration outcomes they say rejected the same kind of retroactive rate change, framing the D.C. Circuit’s approach as a departure from the governing rule.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund), supported by the United States (PBGC/DOJ) and labor/participant amici, argues that MPPAA permits (and in some circumstances requires) the use of actuarially reasonable assumptions to measure unfunded vested benefits and allocate them to withdrawing employers, and it does not freeze assumptions in a way that prevents later correction or adjustment when prior assumptions prove unreasonable or inconsistent with actuarial standards. They contend that the plan’s actuary and trustees must be able to adopt updated assumptions to ensure the withdrawal-liability assessment reflects the plan’s true funding shortfall and protects remaining employers and participants from subsidizing a withdrawing employer. Respondent further argues that the statutory scheme (including PBGC’s role and the presumption of correctness often afforded plan actuarial determinations in MPPAA disputes) favors deference to reasonable actuarial judgments and disfavors a rigid anti-retroactivity rule that could lock in outdated rates and understate liability.
key_precedents: Metz (Second Circuit) (cited by Petitioners as barring retroactive changes to interest-rate assumptions for withdrawal liability)
Jacobson v. Fireman’s Fund Ins. Co., 111 F.3d 2 (2d Cir. 1997) (cited in the record excerpt provided)
Arbitration decisions referenced in the excerpt (two arbitrations described as rejecting the Fund’s position)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh press the best point for Petitioner: §§ 1391 and 1393(b)(1) use valuation-year anchors (“as of” year-end; “most recent complete actuarial valuation”) that serve employer reliance and administrability, and Milwaukee Brewery confirms the measurement-date framework. But that framework does not itself supply a clear textual prohibition on an actuary later selecting, for that same measurement date, the funding-used rate that is the actuary’s “best estimate” and “reasonable in the aggregate” under § 1393(a); reading in a categorical freeze would force use of an assumption shown to violate the statute’s operative command. Justice Barrett’s Russello/§ 1394 negative-implication argument reinforces my minimalist reluctance to imply an across-the-board anti-retroactivity rule for actuarial assumptions when Congress expressly did so for plan amendments, and concerns about “do-overs” can be cabined by a narrow holding requiring proof in arbitration that the post-year-end assumption was (i) actually used for funding purposes and (ii) actuarially reasonable as of the measurement date. Concrete Pipe’s emphasis on actuarial judgment supports deference to a reasonableness inquiry rather than a rigid timing bar, while leaving room to police manipulation through arbitration and judicial review.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed “narrow affirmance” and Justice Barrett’s Russello/§ 1394 negative-implication argument are the most serious points for Respondent, but they do not supply affirmative textual authorization to retroactively increase liability after withdrawal. The text that governs the liability calculation is temporal and fixed—§ 1391 measures unfunded vested benefits “as of the end of the plan year preceding the plan year in which the employer withdraws,” and § 1393(b)(1)’s reference to the “most recent complete actuarial valuation” used for funding purposes is most naturally read to incorporate the valuation-year assumptions actually used for that valuation, not later re-selections. Section 1393(a)’s “best estimate/reasonable” requirement operates within that valuation framework; it does not silently create a power to revise history after the operative event, and § 1394’s express rule about plan amendments cannot overcome the separate, plan-year–anchored commands Congress wrote for withdrawal liability. Concrete Pipe and Milwaukee Brewery confirm deference to actuarial judgment and the measurement-date architecture, but neither supports an implied authority to retroactively swap assumptions post-withdrawal absent a clear statement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is the reliance/administrability concern rooted in §§ 1391 and 1393(b)(1)’s valuation-year language (“as of” year-end; “most recent complete actuarial valuation”), but that argument still does not supply a clear textual prohibition on an actuary later adopting—while still pegged to the same measurement date—the assumption that is actually used for funding and satisfies § 1393(a)’s independent command of “best estimate” and “reasonable in the aggregate.” Justice Barrett’s Russello-style negative implication from § 1394 matters: Congress expressly limited retroactive plan amendments, yet omitted any comparable anti-retroactivity rule for actuarial assumptions, which makes it hard for me as a textualist to infer a categorical freeze. Milwaukee Brewery reinforces the measurement-date framework, but it does not decide the contested step—whether a funding-used assumption shown in arbitration to be reasonable as of that same date must nonetheless be rejected solely because it was selected after year-end. I therefore remain with the Chief’s narrower approach: permit post-year-end use only where the assumption is (1) used for funding purposes and (2) demonstrated to be the reasonable best estimate for the relevant valuation date, leaving manipulation concerns to § 1393(a) and arbitration rather than an implied timing bar.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the reliance/administrability concern: §§ 1391 and 1393(b)(1) speak in valuation-year terms, and employers should not face opportunistic post hoc “do-overs.” But that concern cannot supply a categorical timing bar where § 1393(a) affirmatively conditions permissible assumptions on being, in the aggregate, actuarially reasonable and the actuary’s best estimate for the relevant measurement date—requirements that are hard to square with freezing an assumption later shown unreasonable as of that very date. Justice Barrett’s negative-implication point from § 1394’s express anti-retroactivity rule for plan amendments (and Congress’s silence as to actuarial assumptions) reinforces that we should police manipulation through § 1393(a) and arbitration rather than add an atextual prohibition. Milwaukee Brewery’s measurement-date framework and R.A. Gray’s remedial emphasis support accurate, non-evasive liability calculations over reliance interests when Congress already provided a reasonableness check.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas press the best point for Petitioners: §§ 1391 and 1393(b)(1) contain valuation-year anchors (“as of” year-end; “most recent complete actuarial valuation”) that serve administrability and employer reliance by discouraging after-the-fact “do-overs.” But that timing architecture still doesn’t supply a textual prohibition on using, for the same measurement date, the funding assumptions that § 1393(a)(1) affirmatively requires to be the actuary’s “best estimate” and “reasonable in the aggregate”; reading an implicit freeze risks forcing use of assumptions that fail the statute’s operative standard. Justice Barrett’s Russello/§ 1394 negative-implication argument strengthens the conclusion that Congress knew how to impose an express anti-retroactivity bar and did not do so for actuarial assumptions, so the better coherent reading is to allow post-year-end adoption only when it is genuinely a funding-used, best-estimate assumption for that valuation date and remains reviewable for manipulation in arbitration. Milwaukee Brewery and Concrete Pipe confirm the measurement-date framework and deference to actuarial judgment, but they do not add the missing “no later revisions” rule Petitioners need.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh are right to press the reliance/administrability force of §§ 1391 and 1393(b)(1)’s valuation-year framework, but that structure fixes the measurement date—not a statutory deadline that forbids an actuary from later adopting, for that same date, the assumptions the actuary deems the “best estimate” and “reasonable in the aggregate” under § 1393(a). Their proposed “freeze” reads an atextual timing limitation into “used for purposes of” and risks compelling use of an assumption shown (as of the measurement date) to violate Congress’s operative reasonableness command. Justice Barrett’s Russello/§ 1394 point matters: Congress expressly barred retroactive plan amendments in § 1394 but said nothing comparable about actuarial assumptions, making it hard to justify a categorical anti-retroactivity rule here. Milwaukee Brewery’s emphasis on an “as of” date confirms the temporal anchor, but it does not supply the missing statutory prohibition on post-year-end selection of a funding-used assumption so long as arbitration can test whether it was reasonable as of that anchor date.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow affirmance—allowing post-year-end adoption if the assumption is used for funding and actuarially reasonable as of the measurement date—most directly engages my administrability/reliance concern, but it still treats § 1393(a)’s “best estimate/reasonable” language as a license for after-the-fact re-selection that retroactively increases liability for a completed withdrawal without a clear timing authorization. Justice Barrett’s Russello/§ 1394 negative-implication point is substantial, yet § 1394 speaks to plan amendments, while §§ 1391 and 1393(b)(1) separately establish a plan-year valuation architecture (“as of” year-end; “most recent complete actuarial valuation” used for funding) that, in my view, fixes the governing inputs for that valuation and leaves “reasonableness” policing to arbitration within that temporally bounded framework. Concrete Pipe’s deference to actuarial judgment (as noted by several colleagues) supports reviewing whether the adopted assumptions are reasonable, but it does not compel a regime in which trustees may later revise the assumptions applicable to a past triggering event. Given Congress’s detailed timing structure and the serious retroactivity/reliance consequences, I do not see a sufficiently clear statutory statement authorizing post-withdrawal assumption changes that ratchet up liability for the already-triggered withdrawal.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest textual concern: §§ 1391 and 1393(b)(1) set a valuation-year anchor (“as of” year-end; “most recent complete actuarial valuation”) that promotes reliance and guards against after-the-fact “do-overs.” But that temporal structure does not, on my reading, supply an additional implicit rule that the plan must adhere to whatever assumption happened to be adopted pre-year-end even if it fails § 1393(a)’s operative command that the assumptions used for funding be, in the aggregate, the actuary’s “best estimate” and “reasonable”; importing a categorical freeze risks forcing use of an assumption the statute forbids. The Chief Justice’s § 1394 negative-implication point (Congress expressly limited retroactivity for plan amendments but not actuarial assumptions) reinforces that we should not infer an atextual anti-retroactivity bar here, while Milwaukee Brewery and Concrete Pipe confirm the measurement-date framework and deference to actuarial judgment without compelling the extra step of locking in an unreasonable rate. The better reading is that post-year-end selection is permissible only if it is genuinely a funding assumption and is shown (through arbitration) to have been a reasonable best estimate as of the statutory measurement date, which addresses opportunism without rewriting the text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrow textual proposal—allowing post-year-end adoption if it is the actuary’s best estimate and reasonable as of the measurement date—directly addresses the remedial-purpose concern, but it still underestimates the procedural-fairness and administrability function of §§ 1381(b)(1), 1391, and 1393(b)(1)’s “as of”/“most recent complete actuarial valuation” architecture. Justice Barrett’s Russello/§ 1394 negative-implication argument is substantial, yet I remain unpersuaded that the absence of an express timing bar authorizes retroactive substitution after withdrawal, because the statute separately ties withdrawal liability to a fixed valuation year and to assumptions “used for purposes of” that funding valuation—an anchor that channels disputes into arbitration over the reasonableness of what governed at the relevant time, not a later re-selection. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on R.A. Gray and Milwaukee Brewery reinforces Congress’s broad remedial aims, but those cases do not supply the clear statement I would want before endorsing a regime that permits post-trigger increases that can look like opportunistic “do-overs.” Under my pragmatic approach, the better balance is to enforce § 1393(a) through reasonableness review within the fixed measurement-date framework, rather than allow retroactive changes that weaken notice and predictability for withdrawing employers.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1393(a) directs that withdrawal liability be determined using the plan’s “actuarial assumptions and methods” used for funding purposes, so long as they are “in the aggregate, reasonable,” and nothing in §§ 1381–1405 clearly imposes a rigid rule freezing an interest-rate assumption as of the valuation year if later information shows the assumption was not a reasonable best estimate. Given the statute’s emphasis on actuarial reasonableness and the need to protect remaining employers and participants from subsidizing a withdrawing employer, the better reading allows plans to apply the assumptions the actuary adopts in computing UVBs for the relevant measurement, even if selected after year-end, rather than locking in an outdated rate. Petitioners’ anti-retroactivity rule rests largely on Metz’s “rollover” premise, but that premise is not textually grounded in § 1393(a) and would force courts into highly technical timing disputes better left to actuarial standards and the MPPAA’s dispute-resolution structure. A narrow ruling for Respondent—limited to permitting post-year-end selection of assumptions for the pertinent valuation so long as they are actuarially reasonable and used for funding purposes—best preserves institutional legitimacy while respecting the statutory scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The statutory text ties withdrawal liability to actuarial "assumptions and methods" that are "used for purposes of" funding (26 U.S.C. § 412/ERISA funding rules), and it instructs that the actuary may rely on the "most recent complete actuarial valuation" used for those purposes. 29 U.S.C. § 1393(a), (b)(1). That linkage, combined with MPPAA’s measurement structure that values unfunded vested benefits "as of" the last day of the plan year preceding the withdrawal under the default method, 29 U.S.C. § 1391(b), fixes the relevant assumptions at that measurement date rather than permitting later retroactive revisions to increase liability for a past withdrawal. The Second Circuit’s reading in Metz accords with the statute’s temporal commands and avoids empowering trustees to impose after-the-fact “do-overs” untethered from the valuation year Congress specified. Because the Fund’s retroactive interest-rate change conflicts with the original public meaning of § 1393’s funding-assumptions tie and § 1391’s measurement-date framework, I would reverse.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 29 U.S.C. § 1393(a) requires that withdrawal liability be determined using the plan’s actuarial assumptions and methods "used for purposes of section 1083" and that, in the actuary’s opinion, they be "reasonable" in the aggregate—language that points to actuarial correctness rather than a rigid anti-retroactivity rule. Although 29 U.S.C. § 1391’s allocation provisions measure unfunded vested benefits as of the end of the plan year preceding withdrawal, that timing rule does not expressly freeze the interest-rate assumption in place if the actuary later determines the prior assumption was not actuarially reasonable; locking in an unreasonable rate would understate UVBs and shift costs to remaining employers and participants, a practical consequence the MPPAA was designed to prevent. Milwaukee Brewery confirms the measurement-date framework, but it does not hold that plans are barred from later applying a corrected, actuarially reasonable assumption to that measurement-date calculation. Given Congress’s evident aim to protect plan solvency and prevent employer evasion, I would not extend Metz’s approach into a broad prohibition absent clear statutory text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: MPPAA requires withdrawal liability to be computed using actuarial assumptions and methods that are both those used for funding purposes and “actuarially reasonable,” see 29 U.S.C. § 1393, and that standard would be undermined by a rigid rule freezing assumptions even after they are shown to be unreasonable. This Court has recognized Congress’s strong remedial purpose in MPPAA—to prevent a destabilizing “stampede for the exit doors” and to protect plan participants and remaining employers from bearing the costs of underfunding—PBGC v. R.A. Gray & Co., 467 U.S. 717, 722–725 (1984); Milwaukee Brewery Workers’ Pension Plan v. Jos. Schlitz Brewing Co., 513 U.S. 414, 416–417 (1995). Allowing a plan to correct assumptions to reflect actuarial reasonableness better aligns the assessed liability with the plan’s true unfunded vested benefits and avoids shifting losses onto workers and other contributing employers. While reliance interests matter, MPPAA’s structure and remedial aims favor permitting reasonable corrective updates rather than locking in an unreasonable rate that would understate liability for a past withdrawal.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1393(a)(1) requires withdrawal liability to be determined using actuarial assumptions and methods that, in the aggregate, are “reasonable” and reflect the actuary’s “best estimate” of anticipated experience; that text fits awkwardly with a rigid rule freezing whatever assumptions happened to be used for funding if they later prove unreasonable. Read in statutory context—particularly Congress’s protective purpose in 29 U.S.C. § 1001a(c)—MPPAA is better understood to permit (and sometimes require) an actuary to apply an updated, measurement-date-appropriate best estimate, even if adopted after the valuation year, to avoid systematic understatement that shifts costs to remaining employers and participants. The D.C. Circuit’s approach is more workable because it ties any retroactive application to actuarial reasonableness and the information available as of the measurement date, rather than allowing opportunistic “do-overs” untethered from professional standards. Metz’s contrary rule is not compelled by § 1393’s text, and its anti-retroactivity framing risks locking in demonstrably unreasonable assumptions in a way that undermines the coherence of the withdrawal-liability scheme in §§ 1381–1405.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of 29 U.S.C. § 1393(a) requires that withdrawal liability be determined using actuarial assumptions and methods that are "actuarially reasonable" and, in the actuary’s judgment, reflect the plan’s experience and reasonable expectations—language that points to substantive reasonableness rather than a rigid freeze on a prior year’s interest-rate assumption. Section 1393(b) further confirms Congress did not lock plans to a single valuation-year set of assumptions by expressly permitting use of the "most recent complete actuarial valuation" for funding purposes along with "reasonable estimates" for interim periods, indicating flexibility rather than an anti-retroactivity rule. PBGC guidance likewise indicates § 1393(b)’s reliance on the most recent funding valuation is permissive ("may"), not mandatory, and no PBGC regulation imposes a funding-assumption lockstep, so a plan may adjust assumptions when needed to ensure actuarial reasonableness. While petitioners invoke Metz to argue against retroactive rate changes, the statute’s controlling requirement is actuarial reasonableness under § 1393(a), and I would not read into ERISA/MPPAA a categorical prohibition on post-year-end corrections absent clearer text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under MPPAA, withdrawal liability must be determined using the plan’s “actuarial assumptions and methods” employed “for purposes of section 412 of title 26” and those assumptions must be “actuarially reasonable.” 29 U.S.C. § 1393(a). The better reading, consistent with predictability and reliance interests, is that the relevant assumptions are the ones in effect as of the measurement date/valuation year used to assess unfunded vested benefits, not later “retroactive” revisions that increase liability for a past withdrawal—an approach the Second Circuit adopted in Nat’l Ret. Fund v. Metz Culinary Mgmt., 946 F.3d 146 (2d Cir. 2020). Even if § 1394’s anti-retroactivity clause is textually directed at “plan rule[s] or amendment[s],” Metz persuasively reflects MPPAA’s structure: employers must be able to ascertain the governing inputs at withdrawal, and allowing after-the-fact assumption changes invites manipulation and undermines the statute’s workability. Respondent’s reasonableness/deference arguments (Concrete Pipe) have force, but deference does not authorize retroactive recalculation using assumptions adopted only after the relevant valuation year.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The best reading of 29 U.S.C. § 1393(a) is that withdrawal liability must be calculated using actuarial assumptions that, in the aggregate, are reasonable and reflect the actuary’s best estimate of anticipated experience under the plan, and nothing in that text freezes an interest-rate assumption irrevocably as of the valuation year if it is later determined to be unreasonable. Congress knew how to enact an explicit anti-retroactivity rule—§ 1394 does so for certain “plan rule[s] or amendment[s]” affecting withdrawals—yet it did not extend that limitation to actuarial assumptions, which supports the inference that no such categorical bar exists (Russello v. United States, 464 U.S. 16, 23 (1983)). The Second Circuit’s contrary inference in Metz, drawn from § 1394 rather than § 1393, is not compelled by the statutory text and would overread a provision that by its terms does not govern actuarial assumptions. Given § 1393’s reasonableness/best-estimate commands and the absence of an express statutory prohibition, I would allow the Fund to apply updated assumptions to ensure the assessment reflects the plan’s true unfunded vested benefits, subject to the statutory requirement of actuarial reasonableness.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: MPPAA’s text and structure point to a measurement-date framework that promotes procedural fairness and predictable reliance: withdrawal liability is pegged to the plan’s unfunded vested benefits determined for years ending before the withdrawal year, see 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381(b)(1), 1391, and installment schedules are based on assumptions used for the most recent valuation, § 1399(c)(1)(A)(ii). Reading § 1393(a)(1) to permit trustees to retroactively revise the interest-rate assumption after the valuation year—thereby increasing liability for a past withdrawal—invites opportunistic ‘do-overs’ and undermines the statute’s notice-and-fairness design for employers exiting the plan. While actuarial reasonableness matters, § 1393’s reasonableness constraint is better enforced by challenging unreasonable assumptions through MPPAA’s dispute-resolution process, not by allowing post hoc changes that alter the rules after the employer’s withdrawal. Consistent with Metz (2d Cir.), I would hold that assumptions must be those adopted and used for funding as of the relevant measurement/valuation date, barring retroactive post-year changes to inflate past withdrawal liability.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether ERISA’s MPPAA allows a multiemployer pension plan to retroactively revise the actuarial assumptions (especially the interest/discount rate) used to calculate an employer’s withdrawal liability for a past plan year, thereby increasing the assessed liability after the employer’s withdrawal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA as amended by the Multiemployer Pension Plan Amendments Act of 1980 (MPPAA), principally the withdrawal-liability calculation provisions (e.g., 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1405), including the requirement that withdrawal liability be determined under the plan’s allocable unfunded vested benefits using actuarial assumptions and methods (29 U.S.C. § 1393) and the associated assessment/dispute-resolution framework (including arbitration under 29 U.S.C. § 1401).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (M&K Employee Solutions and related parties) argue that withdrawal liability must be calculated using the plan’s actuarial assumptions and methods as they existed for the relevant measurement period and cannot be increased by the plan later changing those assumptions and applying the change retroactively. They contend that the Fund’s after-the-fact switch in the interest-rate/discount-rate assumption functioned as an impermissible retroactive recalculation that overstated unfunded vested benefits and inflated M&K’s withdrawal liability by millions, contrary to MPPAA’s structure, predictability aims, and at least one circuit’s controlling approach (Metz).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund), supported by the United States and labor/participant amici, argues that MPPAA permits (and sometimes requires) plans to use reasonable actuarial assumptions to best reflect the plan’s experience and expectations, and that trustees/actuaries may correct or update assumptions even if that affects previously issued withdrawal-liability assessments—so long as the assumptions are reasonable under ERISA § 1393 and the statutory dispute-resolution process (arbitration and deferential review) is followed. Respondent characterizes the challenged recalculation as a permissible adjustment to ensure the assessment reflects the plan’s true funding/UVB picture rather than an unlawful retroactive rule change.
key_precedents: Metz (Second Circuit) (cited for the proposition that a plan may not retroactively alter the interest-rate assumption used to calculate withdrawal liability)
Jacobson v. Fireman’s Fund Ins. Co., 111 F.3d 2 (2d Cir. 1997) (mentioned in the record excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is textual: § 1393 speaks in terms of substantive “reasonableness” and contains no explicit temporal “freeze.” But read alongside §§ 1399–1401’s integrated sequence—prompt assessment “as soon as practicable,” pay-now/dispute-later, and arbitration over the assessment issued—the statute presupposes a determinate snapshot capable of being tested in arbitration, not an open-ended power to retroactively swap in later-adopted discount rates after notice has gone out. Justice Alito’s invocation of Concrete Pipe affects the analysis only in the way Justice Kagan notes: it supports deference to actuarial judgments within the statutory process, not authority to reopen a closed valuation year in a one-way-ratchet reassessment. Consistent with R.A. Gray’s caution about retroactivity absent clear authorization, I would adopt a narrow holding barring retroactive application of newly adopted discount-rate assumptions to completed assessments while preserving correction of genuine errors and prospective changes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s best point is structural: §§ 1399–1401 contemplate prompt notice and a pay-now/arbitrate-later regime, and they worry that allowing revised assumptions invites serial reassessments. But that concern cannot justify importing an extra-textual “snapshot” or anti-retroactivity rule where Congress instead wrote a substantive standard in § 1393—whether the assumptions and methods “in the aggregate” are reasonable—and routed disputes to § 1401 arbitration with presumptive validity, as Justice Alito earlier emphasized and as Concrete Pipe’s deference framework supports. R.A. Gray, cited by the Chief Justice, addresses constitutional permissibility of Congress’s retroactive legislation; it does not authorize courts to impose a clear-statement limitation on plan actuaries that the statute’s text does not contain, especially where the statute already supplies finality mechanisms (notice, arbitration, and payment schedules) without freezing assumptions by date. If Petitioners want a categorical ban on using updated discount-rate assumptions for the measurement year, that is a policy judgment Congress could have made expressly; under a strict textualist/originalist approach, I cannot supply it by inference from “as soon as practicable.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is textual: § 1393’s “reasonable (in the aggregate)” standard does not itself supply an explicit timing “freeze,” and I agree courts should be wary of inventing atextual clear-statement rules. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, §§ 1399–1401’s integrated sequence—assessment “as soon as practicable,” pay-now/dispute-later, and arbitration over the assessment actually issued—presupposes a determinate snapshot tied to a closed measurement year, not a continuing power to retroactively swap a new discount rate after notice and thereby convert the process into serial reassessments. Concrete Pipe, which I previously leaned on, fits that structural reading: it supports deference to actuarial judgments within the prescribed assessment-and-arbitration channel, not an implied authority to reopen core assumptions post-assessment in a one-way ratchet against withdrawing employers. R.A. Gray, though addressing Congress’s retroactivity, reinforces the interpretive caution here: absent clearer authorization, I am reluctant to infer that private trustees may impose additional retroactive effects that destabilize finality the statute seems designed to secure.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that § 1393 lacks an express temporal “freeze” and speaks only to substantive reasonableness—does not overcome the MPPAA’s sequenced design in §§ 1399–1401, which depends on a determinate, contemporaneous assessment that can be tested in arbitration rather than repeatedly revised after notice. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the “as soon as practicable” notice plus pay-now/dispute-later regime presupposes finality; otherwise employers (especially smaller, vulnerable ones) face a moving target and serial, one-way-ratchet reassessments they cannot anticipate or mitigate. Justice Alito’s Concrete Pipe/deference point affects my analysis only to confirm that deference attaches to the assumptions used in the issued assessment when reviewed through arbitration—it does not imply authority to retroactively swap assumptions after withdrawal to increase liability. And Roberts’s reliance on R.A. Gray reinforces my reluctance, as a matter of fairness and administrability, to infer retroactive power in private trustees from statutory silence where Congress spoke clearly when it chose retroactive effects.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point remains that § 1393(a)(1) is cast as a substantive “reasonable in the aggregate” requirement and contains no express temporal “freeze,” but text read in context matters: the §§ 1399–1401 sequence (prompt assessment “as soon as practicable,” then pay-now/arbitrate-later) presupposes a determinate snapshot that can be arbitrated, not a moving target subject to retroactive re-rating. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on R.A. Gray usefully reinforces that we should not infer a private retroactive ratchet from silence where Congress has shown it knows how to authorize retroactivity expressly; that doesn’t create an atextual clear-statement rule so much as it confirms the statute’s structural commitment to finality and administrability. Concrete Pipe, as Justice Alito notes, supports deference within the arbitration framework to assumptions actually used in the assessment, but it does not supply authority to reopen a closed measurement year by substituting a later-adopted discount rate after notice has issued. A pragmatic textualist reconciliation is thus: allow prospective assumption changes and bona fide error corrections, but bar retroactive discount-rate swaps that increase an already-triggered, already-assessed liability for a completed year.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is textual: § 1393(a) speaks of “reasonable” assumptions and methods “in the aggregate” and does not expressly freeze inputs as of a particular date. But, as Chief Justice Roberts explains, text must be read in statutory context, and §§ 1399–1401’s command to assess “as soon as practicable” coupled with the pay-now/arbitrate-later regime presupposes a determinate, contemporaneous set of assumptions used to generate the assessment that can then be tested in arbitration—not an ongoing power to retroactively swap discount rates after the fact and reissue liability. Justice Alito’s Concrete Pipe point strengthens that conclusion: deference attaches to the assumptions used in the assessment within the statutory process; it cannot supply authority to reopen closed valuation inputs absent clear statutory authorization. R.A. Gray, though about Congress’s retroactivity, reinforces the interpretive caution here: when retroactive effect is contemplated, Congress knows how to say so, and we should not infer a comparable retroactive ratchet for private trustees from § 1393’s silence.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point remains that § 1393 speaks in terms of substantive “reasonableness” and contains no explicit temporal freeze, and I take that textual silence seriously. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, the surrounding statutory machinery—assessment “as soon as practicable” under § 1399 and the pay-now/arbitrate-later channeling of disputes under § 1401—presupposes a determinate snapshot that can be tested in arbitration, not a rolling authority to reopen a closed measurement year by later substituting a new discount rate after notice issues. Justice Alito’s invocation of Concrete Pipe reinforces deference to contemporaneous actuarial judgments within that process, yet it does not supply affirmative authority for a retroactive reassessment that functions as a one-way ratchet and erodes finality. R.A. Gray’s acceptance of Congress’s limited retroactivity, as Roberts and Barrett note, makes me even more reluctant (as an institutionalist) to infer comparable retroactive power for private trustees from silence rather than clear authorization.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press that § 1393’s text sets a substantive “reasonable in the aggregate” standard and does not expressly impose a temporal “freeze,” but that point weakens once the provision is read in the MPPAA’s integrated scheme. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, §§ 1399–1401 require a prompt assessment and a pay-now/arbitrate-later process that presupposes a determinate snapshot—arbitration tests the assumptions actually used to issue the assessment, not later-selected replacements that reopen a closed measurement year. Concrete Pipe, which Justice Alito initially emphasized, supports deference to actuarial judgments within that statutory sequence; it does not supply authority to retroactively swap discount rates after notice has issued. And Roberts’s reliance on R.A. Gray reinforces that where Congress wanted retroactivity it spoke, so I am reluctant—on a textualist/originalist approach—to infer a private retroactive ratchet from silence in a statute designed for administrability and finality.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point remains that § 1393’s “reasonable in the aggregate” standard contains no express temporal “freeze,” and that disputes over actuarial judgments are routed to § 1401 arbitration. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, the MPPAA’s pay-now/arbitrate-later sequence in §§ 1399–1401 presupposes a determinate, contemporaneous assessment that can be tested in arbitration; allowing later-adopted discount rates to be retroactively swapped in makes arbitration a moving target and turns reassessment into a one-way ratchet against withdrawing employers. Justice Alito’s invocation of Concrete Pipe reinforces deference to the assumptions actually used in the assessment within that channel, not an implied authority to reopen closed valuation years absent clear statutory permission. R.A. Gray, while about Congress’s retroactivity, bolsters the caution Roberts and Barrett articulate: we should not infer comparable retroactive power for private plan actors from silence where the statutory design points toward finality and procedural fairness.

John Roberts.reasoning: MPPAA’s withdrawal-liability scheme contemplates that liability is determined as of the employer’s withdrawal under the plan’s then-applicable “actuarial assumptions and methods” and assessed through the statute’s notice-and-arbitration framework, 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1405, 1393, 1401; allowing trustees to later revise the key discount-rate assumption for a closed measurement year and apply it retroactively would undermine the predictability and finality Congress built into that process. Nothing in § 1393’s command that assumptions be “reasonable” authorizes reopening past-year calculations after an assessment has issued, particularly where doing so functions as a one-way ratchet increasing liability. R.A. Gray upholds Congress’s choice to impose retroactive withdrawal liability by statute, 467 U.S. 717 (1984), but that precedent cuts against implying additional retroactivity by private plan action absent clear statutory authorization. A narrow holding would simply bar retroactive application of a revised discount-rate assumption to a completed withdrawal-liability assessment, leaving plans free to change assumptions prospectively and to correct genuine clerical errors within the existing arbitration mechanism.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The statutory text directs that withdrawal liability be computed using "actuarial assumptions and methods" which, "in the aggregate," are "reasonable" and reflect the plan’s experience and expectations. 29 U.S.C. § 1393(a)(1). Nothing in §§ 1381–1405 or § 1393 fixes the assumptions to those formally adopted by the measurement date as a condition of use, nor does the text single out the discount rate for special anti-retroactivity treatment; the statute instead polices the substance (reasonableness) through arbitration and deferential review under § 1401. Because Congress chose a reasonableness standard rather than a temporal-adoption rule, a plan may apply a later-adopted assumption to the prior measurement year so long as the assumption is reasonable under § 1393 and consistent with the statutory dispute-resolution framework. The Second Circuit’s contrary approach in Metz adds a judicially created timing requirement not found in the enacted text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of ERISA § 1393(a) requires that the actuarial assumptions and methods used to determine unfunded vested benefits “shall, in the aggregate, be reasonable,” and § 1401(a)(3)(B) sets a deferential, arbitration-centered mechanism for challenging those assumptions (unreasonable-in-the-aggregate or significant application error). Nothing in §§ 1381–1405 expressly freezes a plan’s assumptions as of the measurement year in a way that bars a later correction/update that better reflects the plan’s “experience” and “reasonable expectations,” even if it affects a previously issued assessment. Concrete Pipe confirms that trustees and the arbitrator apply this statutory scheme with presumptions favoring the plan on factual/actuarial determinations, while legal questions receive plenary review—but the reasonableness of actuarial assumptions is exactly the kind of determination Congress committed to that deferential process. Given the practical consequences for plan solvency and participants if plans are locked into demonstrably outdated discount rates, I would hold that retroactive adjustment is permissible so long as the assumptions remain reasonable under § 1393 and are vetted through § 1401 arbitration.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: MPPAA’s withdrawal-liability scheme is built around a fixed valuation/measurement period and a prompt, predictable assessment followed by arbitration, see 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1405, 1401; allowing trustees to later change core inputs like the discount rate and apply that change retroactively undermines finality and frustrates the statute’s reliance interests. Section 1393 requires “reasonable” actuarial assumptions, but it does not authorize after-the-fact revisions that increase an employer’s liability for a past year once withdrawal has occurred and the employer’s obligations have effectively crystallized. The Second Circuit’s approach in Metz best fits MPPAA’s structure by preventing post-withdrawal gamesmanship and protecting smaller or vulnerable employers from surprise multimillion-dollar recalculations while leaving plans free to adopt new assumptions prospectively and to resolve disputes through § 1401 arbitration. Fairness and real-world impacts counsel against a rule that lets plans shift financial risk retroactively onto withdrawing employers based on later-selected assumptions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: MPPAA’s withdrawal-liability scheme fixes liability using the plan’s allocable unfunded vested benefits measured as of the relevant valuation/measurement date and determined under the plan’s actuarial “assumptions and methods” applied in a coherent, administrable way. While ERISA § 1393 demands “reasonable” assumptions, that reasonableness inquiry does not authorize trustees to substitute a new discount rate after the measurement date to increase a withdrawn employer’s bill; doing so undermines predictability and effectively functions like a retroactive rule change outside the statutory notice-and-dispute framework (29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1405, 1401). Metz treats this as a legal limit on retroactivity (distinguishing permissible correction of a calculation mistake from a later change in actuarial judgment affecting all employers), and that reading better fits MPPAA’s workability and reliance interests. Arbitration deference under § 1401 cannot cure an assessment method that is unlawful as a matter of statutory structure and timing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The MPPAA’s text contemplates that withdrawal liability is “determined” and then “assessed” under a defined framework, with disputes resolved in arbitration under § 1401—reviewing the reasonableness of the assumptions used, not authorizing trustees to reopen closed valuation years to impose new assumptions retroactively. Section 1393 requires assumptions and methods that are reasonable and the actuary’s best estimate, but nothing in §§ 1381–1405 expressly permits a plan to revise the discount rate after an employer’s withdrawal and apply that change to the already-fixed measurement period to increase liability. Concrete Pipe underscores both the inevitable “imprecision” in actuarial choices and Congress’s choice to channel challenges through arbitration with presumptions, 508 U.S. at 629, 635–636—supporting using the contemporaneous assumptions subjected to that process rather than later, retroactive recalculations. Given the statute’s structure and the rule-of-law values of predictability and finality inherent in a mandatory assessment/arbitration scheme, I would not infer a power to impose retroactive assumption changes absent clear congressional authorization.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: MPPAA’s structure contemplates that withdrawal liability is fixed by a plan-year measurement of “unfunded vested benefits,” calculated using the plan’s actuarial “assumptions and methods” adopted for that determination and then channeled through a prompt notice-and-arbitration process. See 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1401, 1393; Concrete Pipe & Prods. of Cal., Inc. v. Constr. Laborers Pension Tr. for S. Cal., 508 U.S. 602 (1993) (emphasizing the statutory assessment/arbitration framework). Allowing trustees to retroactively revise the discount rate after an employer’s withdrawal and after an assessment issues would undermine predictability and workability, inviting repeated re-assessments and upsetting settled expectations in a way Congress did not clearly authorize. PBGC v. R.A. Gray & Co., 467 U.S. 717 (1984), upheld Congress’s own limited retroactivity for withdrawal liability, but it does not suggest that private plans may create retroactivity by changing assumptions post hoc; absent clear statutory text, judicial restraint counsels against reading MPPAA to permit that.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The MPPAA’s withdrawal-liability scheme is built around a measurement-date “snapshot” of allocable unfunded vested benefits, and § 1393’s requirement that assumptions be “reasonable” does not clearly authorize trustees to revise an interest/discount-rate assumption after that measurement date and then apply it to a completed plan year to increase an already-triggered § 1381 liability. Reading § 1393 in context with §§ 1381–1405 and the statute’s pay-now-dispute-later framework (§ 1401), permitting retroactive assumption changes would undermine predictability and invite post-withdrawal recalculations untethered to the assessment structure Congress prescribed. The Second Circuit’s approach in Metz—treating the discount-rate assumption in effect as of the last day of the year preceding withdrawal as fixed for liabilities measured as of that date—best accords with the statute’s temporal structure and is reinforced by § 1394(a)’s anti-retroactivity principle for post-snapshot changes. Because the Act does not speak with sufficient clarity to permit retroactive increases via later-adopted actuarial assumptions, I would hold the Fund’s retroactive change impermissible and vote for Petitioners.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: MPPAA’s structure contemplates a determinate, snapshot-style calculation of withdrawal liability tied to the plan year and the plan’s allocable unfunded vested benefits, with notice “as soon as practicable” and a pay-now/dispute-later arbitration regime under §§ 1399–1401; allowing trustees to later revise core actuarial inputs for that same measurement period would undermine predictability and procedural fairness. Although § 1393 requires “reasonable” actuarial assumptions, that reasonableness inquiry is best applied to the assumptions in effect for the relevant valuation/measurement date—not used as a license for retroactive recalculation that increases liability after withdrawal. The Second Circuit’s Metz approach—rejecting retroactive interest/discount-rate changes that increase a withdrawing employer’s liability—better aligns with MPPAA’s reliance interests and avoids practical due-process concerns that arise when plans can inflate assessments long after withdrawal. Section 1394(a)’s bar on retroactive application of post-snapshot plan rule changes further reinforces Congress’s intent that post-withdrawal changes not be used to increase liability over employer objection.
